newsitem.title: USA: Stocks mixed, bonds fall before long weekend, dollar up.
newsitem.headline: Stocks mixed, bonds fall before long weekend, dollar up.

text.p: Stock prices ended mixed on Thursday as investors favored small companies' shares at the expense of blue-chips, while bonds slid ahead of the long Memorial Day weekend.
The dollar rose again on Japanese officials' vocal support of their central bank's low interest rate policy and a potential shake-up at Britain's central bank.
Coffee prices continued to rise as speculators pushed futures prices to new life-of-contract highs.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 32.56 points at 7,258.13.
The broader market showed some strength, with advancing issues leading declines 1,271 to 1,175 on active volume of 426 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The negative tone for blue chips came on the heels of a rally of more than 100 points earlier this week amid euphoria surrounding the Federal Reserve decision to keep interest rates unchanged after raising them a month earlier.

"We're been giving back some of the gains from that euphoric spike up," said said Scott Bleier, chief market strategist for Prime Charter Ltd. "But with the wild volatility in the market, which is here to stay, we need to digest gains in order to lessen the volatility above 7000."
The Dow losses were also driven by weakness in bonds, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond rising briefly to the 7 percent level.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 11/32, which raised its yield to 6.99 percent from Wednesday's 6.96 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Analysts said the bond market was erratic as traders seemed confused after the Fed released the minutes from its March 25 policy-setting meeting.
The Fed panel voted 10-0 to move to a neutral monetary policy at the same time it raised rates.

The minutes, released with the customary six-week lag, painted a picture of a central bank increasingly worried about the risk of faster inflation, but divided over how big a danger that posed to the economy.
"When negative comments were published from the minutes, bonds sold off. When positive comments came out, bonds came back," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp.
The dollar rose to 116.10 Japanese yen from 114.35 late Wednesday and edged up to 1.6943 German marks from 1.6931. The British pound fell sharply to $1.6249 from $1.6455.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery rose as high as 265.00 cents a pound before easing back to close at 260.30 cents, up 7.20 cents.
Copper prices in New York continued to post gains, with futures posting life-of-contract highs for the third time in a week with prices now at their highest levels in almost a year.
Copper for July delivery at the COMEX closed at 118.95 cents a pound, up 0.75 cent.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended little changed in quiet trade ahead of the Memorial Day weekend. Crude oil for July delivery ended unchanged at $21.86 a barrel.
Gasoline for July delivery closed 0.23 cent a gallon higher at 65.10 cents and July heating oil rose 0.17 cent a gallon to 57.85 cents.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100, which raced to an intraday trading high of 4,661.7, a mere 32 points below its record closing peak, finished 9.8 points firmer at 4,651.8. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average index finished 35.41 points, or 0.18 percent, higher at 19,877.39.
